# Parallel implementations and duplicated logic: definitions, detection, and when duplication is acceptable

## Summary
"Parallel implementations" in a codebase come in four detectable-to-judgmental forms — a second helper beside an existing one, a hand-rolled version of a library function, two drifting code paths for one behavior, and literal copy-paste duplication — and they span the same scale that clone research calls Type-1 (exact token copies) through Type-4 (same behavior, different code), with only the first two reliably detectable by tools [s4][s5][s11]. Exact copy-paste is mechanically gateable (token-based detectors like jscpd or PMD CPD, ideally as a "new-clone-only" baseline gate rather than a percentage threshold), renamed/parallel helpers are detectable as review leads with higher false positives, and behavioral duplication (drift, hand-rolled library functions) is fundamentally a judgment call that tools can only surface [s4][s5][s6][s7][s11]. Evidence shows AI coding agents produce these systematically: in a 3,000-turn benchmark audit agents left duplicated logic in 50.8% of task chains by turn 5, and industry data shows cloned lines of changed code rising while refactoring shares fall [s1][s3][s15].

## Assumptions
- The question is asked in the context of a review agent whose rubric has two check types — deterministic gates over the diff and yes/no judgment questions — so each indicator below is labeled with which of those it fits. The code examples are illustrative reconstructions by the author, except the money-formatting case, which is a lightly abridged retelling of a documented incident [s2].
- The full text of the FSE 2025 paper "An Empirical Study of Code Clones from Commercial AI Code Generators" (dl.acm.org) returned HTTP 403, so only its existence, venue, and authorship could be verified [s19][s22]; no specific measurements from it are cited here.
- The body of the Google Testing Blog post "Don't DRY Your Code Prematurely" did not render in the fetched page (only site navigation), so no claims from it are included.
- GitClear's 2023→2026 duplication figures are cited as reported by a secondary source that quotes GitClear [s3], not from GitClear's own 2026 report page, which was not fetched.

## Findings

### Indicator 1: A second helper beside an existing one (parallel implementation of an existing utility)

**Definition.** A new function that does the job of a function that already exists in the repo — "a small helper" introduced next to the one that already covers the requirement. The defining property is that both copies encode the same *behavior*; the harm is not the extra lines but "the loss of a single place to change behavior": a fix must now be applied in two places, and one will be missed [s2].

**Code example (from a documented agent incident).** The repo already exported `formatCurrency()` in `packages/currency/src/format.ts`, which applied the finance-approved rounding rule (half-even) after a real fractional-cents incident. An agent added `formatMoneyCents()` in a new `pricing.ts` that did the same job but rounded half-up. Nothing failed in the PR; the divergence "would have failed quietly, months later, on a specific refund total" [s2].

**How a reviewer shows it from the diff.** The duplication checker's method: "When a PR adds something new, check if something similar already exists: existing helpers, imported dependencies, type definitions, components. Search the codebase," and when a match is found, "Don't argue. Show where it already lives" — i.e., cite the existing function's file and line [s23]. Search *by behavior, not just the name the author invented* (e.g., grep for `round|currency|money|cents`), and list what is already exported on the public surface (`rg -n "export .*format"`) [s2]. For agent-written PRs, the transcript check is the evidence: look for a search or read of the existing helper's file *before* the write that created the twin — no search means the agent never looked; a read followed by a twin means it looked and rewrote anyway [s3].

**Mechanical detection.** Partially. Token/AST similarity over functions catches renamed copies: jscpd's `--similarity` normalizes each function's syntax tree (called-function names and operators stay, local names and literals become markers) and reports pairs from 0.8 similarity up, and is explicitly recommended as a post-session/CI check alongside `jscpd --changed --fail-on-new-clones` [s3][s4][s5]. Import boundaries / dependency rules can make "where this logic is allowed to live" a hard CI rule — for shared domains like money, dates, and identifiers, "a dependency rule or an import boundary turns 'please remember' into something the CI enforces" [s2]. Pure semantic reuse ("this new helper duplicates that one") is *not* reliably mechanical: jscpd's experimental `--semantic` embedding mode reports candidate pairs but "a similarity score says that two functions look alike to the model, and it cannot tell whether they behave alike, so review a pair before you merge" [s4][s5]. Fits a gate when framed as "new exact/AST clone introduced by this diff"; fits a per-finding yes/no question ("does this new helper duplicate an existing one, and if so, why can't the existing one be used?") in general.

**False positives.** Moderate-to-high if you gate on it. Exact (Type-1) clones are "nearly always a copy that should be a shared function, and the result is stable enough for a baseline," but renamed matches "find more and longer clones" and should be "read as leads to check, since some parametric similarity is idiomatic" [s4][s5]. Legitimate parallel helpers exist and are acceptable when the two functions "encode genuinely different policies" — the difference must be visible in the names, documented at both sites, and pinned by a test; "if you cannot articulate the policy difference in one sentence, you do not have two functions; you have one function and a future bug" [s2].

### Indicator 2: A hand-rolled version of a library function

**Definition.** Re-implementing, locally, functionality that a dependency, standard library, or generated artifact already provides — "reimplemented string helpers when the dependency is already available," "hand-written interfaces that duplicate generated types," "a new wrapper that could be a call to an existing function" [s23]. The variant of indicator 1 where the "existing thing" is a dependency rather than a repo utility.

**Code example.** Adding a local `slugify()` that strips accents and dashes a string, when the codebase already depends on a slug library (or `Intl`/stdlib equivalents); or writing a hand-rolled debounce when a utility package is already imported elsewhere.

**How a reviewer shows it from the diff.** Cite the import that already provides the behavior, plus the local reimplementation: "a new wrapper that could be a call to an existing function" is exactly the catch list of the duplication-checker role, whose evidence rule is to show the existing location rather than argue [s23]. In agent contexts, this is the canonical failure mode — "Suppose an agent adds an email validator to a form. Another version lives in `utils/`, one sits in `services/`" — and the fix is to make existing utilities *findable* (public surface, helper lists in AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md), because agents work from retrieval, not a mental map of the codebase [s2].

**Mechanical detection.** Partially, and mostly indirectly. A deterministic gate can enforce that certain behaviors are *only* reachable through a designated module (import boundaries: force "money, time, and identifier logic to live in a single package") [s2]; a lint rule can flag known hand-rolled patterns (e.g., a naive debounce loop) but cannot generally recognize semantic reimplementation of a library function. `--semantic` clone detection (code-embedding model comparing whole functions, within or across languages) is the closest mechanical net, with the same review-before-acting caveat [s4][s5]. Otherwise this is judgment: the reviewer must know the dependency surface the project has committed to.

**False positives.** High if gated mechanically — a locally specialized variant of a library function (different defaults, size constraints, no-dependency policy, performance requirements) is common and can be correct. The same "one sentence" test applies: a defensible hand-rolled version has an articulable reason (bundle size, environment, behavior difference) stated at the site; a silent one is the bug [s2].

### Indicator 3: Two code paths for one behavior that drift (behavioral duplication / "drift")

**Definition.** "Duplication is when there's a single behavior that's specified in two or more places" — not when two pieces of code are textually identical. The test: "if I changed one piece of code in order to meet a new requirement, would it be logically necessary to update the other piece of code the same way? If so, then the two pieces of code are probably duplicates of each other, even if their behavior is not achieved using the same exact syntax" [s11]. Drift is what happens when the two copies diverge: "segments of code initially supposed to do the same thing may grow apart undetected upon further refactoring," at which point automated tools "will no longer recognise these blocks as duplicates" [s7].

**Code example.** `save(user)` in `save-account.js` and `save-user.js` share the row-mapping, timestamp, DB write, and audit call, but one acquired `if (!row.id) throw new Error('id')` after a bug report — a Type-3 near-miss clone where "a validation line inserted here, a logging call dropped there" [s4]. The money case is the drift made concrete: identical-shaped formatters, one later changed to half-even, the twin still half-up [s2].

**How a reviewer shows it from the diff.** This is the least mechanical indicator. The reviewer cites both sites of the behavior and the *difference* between them — the one-sided change (the added guard, the changed default, the different rounding) — and argues with the change-propagation question: a fix to behavior X would have to be made in two files [s11][s2]. The documented cost model: every caller of the shared behavior "must be applied in two places; one will be missed," and domain rules "can silently diverge under a different default" [s2]. For agent PRs, a test can make drift visible: the same input run through both paths and compared — in the money case, "nothing failed in the pull request" until a specific refund total exposed the rounding mismatch [s2].

**Mechanical detection.** Weak. A token-window detector sees drift as fragmentation: "a token-window detector sees it as two shorter exact clones with a gap between them," and `--max-gap-lines N` can merge those pieces into one reported clone with a similarity score (one inserted line in a 150-token block reads ~0.9) [s4][s5]. `--similarity` (whole-function AST comparison) reaches scattered edits a token window misses [s4][s5]. But Type-4 — "two functions that compute the same result with different statements" — is "out of their reach, as they are for every token-based detector"; only the experimental semantic pass approaches it, and "each pair it reports still needs a review" [s5][s4]. So: *detectable as leads, judgmental as findings.* This is the indicator that belongs in the yes/no decision model ("do these two paths implement the same behavior, and would a fix to one have to be mirrored in the other?"), not in the deterministic gate.

**False positives.** As a gate, very high — identical-looking code that "actually serve[s] different purposes and lead[s] separate lives" is not duplication, and "to 'DRY up' these identical-looking pieces of code would create new problems, like handcuffing two people together who need to walk in two different directions" [s11]. As a review lead, the false-positive cost is a wasted look; as a required-failure gate, it will fire on legitimate variants (different policies, different layers, frontend/backend pairs that are deliberately parallel).

### Indicator 4: Copy-paste duplication (token clones)

**Definition.** Repeated sequences of code: the clone taxonomy sorts duplicates "into four types by how much the copies have drifted apart" — Type-1 exact (differ only in whitespace/layout/comments), Type-2 renamed/parameterized (identifiers, literals, annotations changed), Type-3 near-miss (statements added/removed/changed in the middle), Type-4 semantic (everything but the behavior differs) [s4]. The gateable core is Type-1/Type-2: "a clone is a repeated sequence of language tokens, not a repeated run of characters," found by a rolling Rabin-Karp hash over language-specific token streams with `--min-tokens`/`--min-lines` thresholds [s5]. PMD's CPD is the same class of tool: token-based, `--minimum-tokens` required, and "by default, CPD finds identical duplicates" [s7].

**Code example.** The classic Type-2 renamed clone:

```js
// cart.js
export function cartTotal(items, taxRate) {
  let subtotal = 0;
  for (const item of items) subtotal += item.price * item.quantity;
  const tax = subtotal * taxRate;
  return { subtotal, tax, total: subtotal + tax };
}
// basket.js — same structure, renamed identifiers/literals
export function basketTotal(entries, vatRate) {
  let net = 0;
  for (const entry of entries) net += entry.price * entry.quantity;
  const vat = net * vatRate;
  return { net, vat, gross: net + vat };
}
```

[Source page's own example [s4]]

**How a reviewer shows it from the diff.** The reviewer (or the gate) cites both file:line ranges of the repeated block — that is the native output shape of these tools: jscpd prints `Clone found (javascript, renamed)` with both ranges and token counts [s4], CPD reports file + line + token count per clone [s7]. A diff-specific tool exists for exactly this: cccv "finds what parts of a diff were copy/pasted from elsewhere in the project" precisely "because copy/pasted code is impossible to spot at code review time" — `git diff master | cccv` with tunables `min-hunk-size` (default 2 consecutive lines), `min-line-length` (default 10), and regex exclusions [s8]. Git itself supports origin-of-lines queries (blame-based), and the standard PR workflow is branch vs. base-ref comparison [s6][s8].

**Mechanical detection.** Fully — this is the one indicator that is a clean deterministic gate. jscpd: exact clones by default, `--ignore-identifiers`/`--ignore-literals` for renamed [s4][s5]; PMD CPD: `--minimum-tokens 100 --dir src`, exits non-zero (status 4) when duplicates are found "to ease CPD integration into scripts or hooks" [s7]. For a PR gate specifically, the key design is the baseline: record existing clone fingerprints (hash of fragment content; "nothing about paths or line numbers goes into the hash, so moving a file, shifting lines… leaves the gate quiet") and "fail only when a change adds a clone" — `jscpd --baseline-from-ref origin/main --fail-on-new-clones`, or `--changed` to report only clones touching changed files; new clones surface at error level in SARIF while pre-existing ones stay warnings, so "GitHub code scanning highlights only the regression" [s6].

**False positives.** Low at sufficient token counts for Type-1, which is why "in CI, gate on Type-1. Exact clones are unambiguous and stable across runs, which is what a failing check needs" [s4][s5]. Known mechanical false-positive sources and their documented fixes: duplicated annotations in Java/C# ("this causes false positives" → `--ignore-annotations`) [s7]; comment/string content (handled by language-aware tokenization, which is what "buys… precision within that scope: fewer false positives from comments and strings") [s5]; boilerplate like license headers (`--ignore-pattern` / `jscpd:ignore-start`) [s5]; identical-looking but semantically independent code (the "two people walking in two different directions" case — a semantic false positive of any textual detector) [s11]. The bigger practical failure mode is a mis-set *percentage threshold*: "set high, it lets a fresh copy-paste through under the limit; set low, it trips on legacy code the change never touched" — which is exactly why the baseline/new-clone gate replaces it for PRs [s6].

### Detection tools, summarized

- **jscpd** (220+ languages, single binary, Rust engine, SARIF/JSON/HTML reporters, GitHub Action, MCP server): token-based Type-1 by default; `--ignore-identifiers/--ignore-literals/--ignore-annotations` for Type-2; `--max-gap-lines` and `--similarity` (whole-function AST, 15 languages) for Type-3; experimental `--semantic` embeddings for Type-4; `--kind` filters reported categories [s4][s5]. PR-gating: baseline file with content fingerprints, `--fail-on-new-clones [N]` (N = budget of allowed new clones), `--baseline-from-ref` (git ref as baseline, no committed file), `--changed` (only clones in changed files, baseline auto-saved from HEAD) [s6]. A twin "rewritten from scratch" can still pass the token checks, which is why it is paired with a fresh-context review prompt that lists new functions and searches for equivalents [s3].
- **PMD CPD**: token detector with `--minimum-tokens` (required), per-language ignore flags; exits 4 on duplication, 5 on lexing errors (a documented false-*negative* mode, since an unlexable file reports no clones); suppression via `CPD-OFF`/`CPD-ON` comments; and an explicit stance: "use CPD to help remove duplicates, not to help keep duplicates in sync" [s7].
- **cccv**: the narrow, diff-scoped option — finds lines in the diff that were copy/pasted from elsewhere in the project; "relies on default git diff output format" and is tuned with hunk-size/line-length/exclusion config [s8].
- **Review-agent skills** institutionalize the judgment half: the duplication-checker role (search for similar existing helpers/dependencies/types/components; "Don't argue. Show where it already lives"; scope limited to duplication only) [s16][s23]; similar reuse-reviewer roles are committed in other open-source repos as well (e.g., compound-engineering-plugin), but those pages were not fetched, so they are mentioned only as unverified observations.

### The heuristics: rule of three, DRY, wrong abstraction

- **Rule of three.** "A code refactoring rule of thumb… two instances of similar code do not require refactoring, but when similar code is used three times, it should be extracted into a new procedure," popularized by Martin Fowler and attributed to Don Roberts; it encodes the judgment that maintenance cost outweighs refactoring risk at three copies, while premature extraction "risks selecting a wrong abstraction" [s17]. It is genuinely contested: one practitioner treats it as a guard on "Advanced Beginners… greedily removing all duplication" before they can distinguish accidental from essential duplication, and disagrees with strict waiting [s9]; another argues the *count* of copies is not the meaningful factor at all — a hard-to-see, high-traffic *double* duplication is worse than an obvious, low-traffic triple, and the decision should be severity (discoverability/overhead/traffic) plus whether the de-duplicated version is actually better [s11].
- **DRY.** The principle, as formulated by Hunt and Thomas: "Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system," aimed at "reducing repetition of information which is likely to change" [s24]. Note the target is *knowledge likely to change* — which is why identical code expressing different, independently-changing behaviors is not a DRY violation [s11][s24].
- **Wrong abstraction.** Sandi Metz's "duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction": a premature extraction acquires a parameter, then a conditional, then another, until the shared code "interleaves a number of vaguely associated ideas… hard to understand and easy to break"; the remedy when an abstraction is proved wrong is to inline it and "re-introduce duplication" to see the real seams [s10]. The AHA ("avoid hasty abstractions") variant in the DRY literature reaches the same place: abstract "when the duplication itself has become the barrier and it is known how the abstraction needs to function," explicitly rooted in Metz's "prefer duplication over the wrong abstraction" [s24]. Counterweight: the rule-of-three critic's warning that these refrains have "treated duplication in an oversimplified way," and that the real failure is extracting *too early*, not duplicating [s11].

### When duplication is acceptable

Collected from the sources, the legitimate duplication cases are:

1. **Deliberately different policies.** Two functions that intentionally encode different behaviors (e.g., display rounding vs. exact ledger precision) are fine when "the difference should be visible in the names, documented at both sites, and covered by a test that pins the divergent behavior" — articulable in one sentence, or it isn't two functions [s2].
2. **Code that will not change.** "If the code may never change in the future, then this is not a problem" (PMD's stated exemption); suppression comments (`CPD-OFF`) exist for exactly these cases [s7].
3. **Low-severity duplication.** High proximity + high similarity + low change-traffic: "two short lines of very similar code, located right next to each other, are very easy to keep in sync" [s11]; and when "the de-duplicated version unavoidably results in code that's so generalized that it's virtually impossible to understand," the duplicate "may be the lesser of two evils" [s11].
4. **Idiomatic parametric similarity.** "Some parametric similarity is idiomatic" — the renamed-clone false-positive class that's fine as long as no shared behavior exists [s4].
5. **The learning/uncertainty window.** Waiting for a second or third instance so the abstraction matches a pattern actually observed rather than an imagined one [s17][s9], with inlining as the documented exit when the abstraction turns out wrong [s10][s9].

### Evidence: AI-generated code duplicating existing utilities

- **RepoReuse (Ma et al., arXiv 2609.35357, Sep 2026)** — a multi-turn benchmark auditing code reuse in real repositories, "an audit over 3,000 turns shows that agents progressively stop exploring relevant repository code, reuse their own history less even when it is fully in the workspace, and leave duplicated logic in 50.8% of task chains by turn 5 — all while pass rates barely move. Such deficiencies are invisible to pass rates" [s1]. Detailed measurements: agents read 83.6% of the relevant repository code on the first task of a chain and 35.4% by the fifth; the share of chains containing a re-implemented function rose from 13.8% to 50.8%; *every* configuration read at least 98.9% of the functions it had written on earlier turns yet reused only 67.0–86.4% of them — "the bottleneck is the agent's disposition, not its access to the code"; and this occurred *with* an instruction in every run to find and reuse existing modules [s3]. Giving the agent a list of earlier functions' module/name/signature/behavior raised reuse from 30.0% to 67.8%, suggesting discoverability (not just instructions) is the lever [s3].
- **A 617-PR study in one Python repository** (cited by the secondary source above): "agent-written changes scored 0.2867 on a redundancy measure against 0.1532 for human ones" [s3].
- **GitClear industry data.** Over 211M changed lines analyzed (2020–2024), "lines classified as 'copy/pasted' (cloned) rose from 8.3% to 12.3%" between 2021 and 2024, while refactoring's share of changed lines "sank from 25% of changed lines in 2021, to less than 10% in 2024"; the 2025 report reports "4x more code cloning" and "copy/paste" exceeding "moved" code "for the first time in history" [s15]. For 2023→2026 (YTD), GitClear counted duplicated blocks of 5+ lines rising from 40.3 to 73.0 per million changed lines, an 81% increase "it ties to growing AI authorship" (as reported by the secondary source [s3]; GitClear's own 2026 report was not fetched).
- **Peer-reviewed existence check.** "An Empirical Study of Code Clones from Commercial AI Code Generators" was a FSE 2025 research paper (Wu, Hu, Fan, Qiao, Huang, Li, Zheng, Lyu) with published reproducibility code — evidence that clone analysis of commercial AI code generators is an active empirical area — but its abstract/full text was inaccessible (HTTP 403), so its specific findings are unverified here [s19][s22].
- **Mechanism (why agents do it).** Four forces, per the documented incident: local context bias (the existing utility is too far away to be in context), name mismatch (fuzzy search misses `formatCurrency` when the agent thinks "money cents"), reward for completion (a self-contained helper is "the lowest-risk path to a green build"), and barrel exports hiding the source of an already-public function [s2]. The four-cause taxonomy with transcript-level tests: never searched / searched and rewrote anyway / no map of where shared code lives / helper dropped out of context — with the practical consequence that "a duplicate check after the session catches the twins every rule misses," hence post-session `jscpd --changed --fail-on-new-clones` plus a review prompt in fresh context [s3].
- **Mitigations with the evidence:** require the agent to search and *report the path of any existing function considered* before writing a helper; keep a current map of shared-code locations in the agent's instruction file; and for high-value domains (money, dates, identifiers) enforce a single allowed home via dependency/import rules "which eliminates the most damaging class of duplicated helpers" — acknowledging that lint "cannot recognize every semantic duplicate" [s2].

### Rubric mapping (gate vs. judgment)

| Indicator | Deterministic gate? | Yes/no question? | False-positive risk if gated |
|---|---|---|---|
| Copy-paste (Type-1, new clones in diff) | Yes — jscpd `--baseline-from-ref --fail-on-new-clones` / CPD / cccv [s6][s7][s8] | Fallback for small blocks | Low at adequate token counts [s4][s5] |
| Renamed clone (Type-2) | No as a hard fail — "leads to check" [s4] | Yes | Medium-high; idiomatic parametric code [s4][s7] |
| Near-miss / drift (Type-3) | No — fragmentary by design [s4][s5] | Yes, with both sites cited [s11] | High if gated [s11] |
| Second helper beside existing one | Partially — import boundaries for designated domains [s2]; `--similarity` as lead | Yes — "show where it already lives" [s23] | Medium [s2] |
| Hand-rolled library function | Partially — same boundary rules [s2]; `--semantic` as lead [s4] | Yes | High if gated [s2] |
| Behavioral duplication (Type-4 / drift of one behavior) | No — out of reach of token detectors [s5] | Yes — change-propagation test [s11] | High [s11] |
